title: Buddy Rich - Wikipedia
notes: Read to character 100,000 of 107,164. Bernard 'Buddy' Rich, born 30 September 1917, Sheepshead Bay, Brooklyn; died 2 April 1987, Los Angeles, of 'unexpected respiratory and cardiac failure' after treatment for a malignant brain tumour removed at UCLA on 16 March. Vaudeville from 18 months, in a sailor suit; headlining as 'Baby Traps the Drum Wonder' by four. Joe Marsala 1937; Bunny Berigan, Artie Shaw; Tommy Dorsey 1939-42, 1945, 1954-55; Marines 1942-44; Benny Carter 1942; his own orchestra 1945-48 with Sinatra's backing; Harry James 1953-62, 1964, 1965; JATP, Les Brown, Charlie Ventura, Count Basie, Bird and Diz (1950); his own big band from 1966 to his death. 'He usually held his sticks with the traditional grip', matched for 'floor toms around the drum set' in cross-stickings; speed, power, single-stroke rolls; 'the stick-trick, a fast roll performed by slapping two drumsticks together in a circular motion'; a single-stroke roll on the snare moved toward the rim as it got quieter, 'Then he would reverse the effect and slowly move towards the center of the snare while increasing power.' Never read music; Bobby Shew: 'He'd only have to listen to a chart once and he'd have it memorized.' Henry Adler: Rich 'didn't practice'; co-wrote Buddy Rich's Modern Interpretation of Snare Drum Rudiments (1942). Rich: 'I don't put much emphasis on practice anyhow.' Cited Gene Krupa, Jo Jones, Chick Webb, Ray McKinley, Ray Bauduc and Sid Catlett. Influenced Dave Weckl, Vinnie Colaiuta, Simon Phillips, Hal Blaine, John Bonham, Carl Palmer, Ian Paice, Max Weinberg; Travis Barker called him the greatest; Phil Collins 'stopped using two bass drums and started playing the hi-hat' after reading his view of it. Krupa: 'the greatest drummer ever to have drawn breath.' Slingerland in the 1960s-70s, sometimes a Fibes snare; 'switched exclusively to Ludwig in the late 1970s through the early 1980s'; from 1983 a 1940s Slingerland Radio King to his death; also Rogers. Typical set: 14x24 bass drum, 9x13 mounted tom, two 16x16 floor toms, 5.5x14 snare; Avedis Zildjian 14-inch New Beat hats, 20-inch medium ride, 8-inch splash, two 18-inch crashes. Drum battles with Krupa, Ed Shaughnessy, Louie Bellson; Animal on The Muppet Show (1981). Married Marie Allison 1953; daughter Cathy a singer. Krupa and Rich (1956), Rich versus Roach (1959), Swingin' New Big Band (1966, the West Side Story medley arranged by Bill Reddie), Rich a la Rakha (1968), Mercy, Mercy (1968, 'finest all-round recording' of the big band). Berklee honorary doctorate 1980; PAS Hall of Fame 1986. Burning for Buddy (1994), produced by Neil Peart.

title: Steve Fidyk, 'Buddy Rich: Style & Analysis' (Modern Drummer, 17 October 2012)
notes: His sound 'supportive' but cutting through each section of the band 'like a razor blade'. Kit: 14x24 bass drum with a moleskin patch and a wooden beater, 9x13 rack tom, two 16x16 floor toms, 5x14 snare; Avedis Zildjian 20-inch ride, two 18-inch crashes, 14-inch hi-hats, a 6-inch splash; Remo Coated Diplomat heads; wood-tip sticks a little heavier than a 7A. His time 'right down the middle of the beat'; Jim Chapin: the most accurate beat-to-beat time he ever heard. 'Listen to the way he interprets section and ensemble figures' to hear 'a supreme, articulate accompanist'. Chelsea Bridge (Mercy, Mercy) for his hi-hat phrasing; Quiet Please (Dorsey, 1940) for early tom and snare soloing; Come Back to Me (Sammy Davis Jr., The Sounds of '66); the opening of the West Side Story medley solo transcribed in four PDFs, which were not read.

title: Les Tomkins, interview with Buddy Rich (Crescendo, March 1968; National Jazz Archive, 'Buddy Rich: Interview 2')
notes: Two bass drums: 'a gimmick, that's all'; 'If you're playing two bass drums, you can't play the hi-hat', which means 'leaving off one of the most important sounds in drumming.' 'I play with my heart'; 'I play exactly the way I feel.' Diz, Bird, Pres and Tatum 'played themselves-they didn't play the horn'; 'we have everybody playing like everybody else.' Of Herb Alpert: 'He's got nine men; I've got 17.' Don Ellis 'maybe ... a little too advanced for the ear'.

title: Les Tomkins, interview with Buddy Rich (Jazz Professional; National Jazz Archive, 'Buddy Rich: Interview 1')
notes: The archive dates it 1 January 1980, its copyright notice 1968: the date is unsettled. 'The whole basic point of drumming is to keep time.' 'I rush-and there's a purpose for rushing.' 'Rushing is part of the excitement of playing.' 'It drives me crazy when I hear somebody slow down; I can't tolerate that.' 'if the tempo is absolutely perfect, it's so mechanical that it can't possibly swing.' 'I like a very tight drum'; the bass drum has 'a front head and a back head'; of Krupa's recordings, 'His bass drum was filled with paper-so that only Gene knew what he was playing.' 'The greatest soloist I ever heard on drums was Chick Webb'; 'the greatest drummer that ever lived was Chick Webb'; 'He had fantastic speed.' The great drummers 'never practised'; 'I never felt there was anybody qualified to teach me.' Ronnie Verrell 'just an excellent big-band drummer'.

title: Les Tomkins, interview with Buddy Rich (Jazz Professional; National Jazz Archive, 'Buddy Rich: Interview 1' page 1621493)
notes: Dated 1 January 1981 by the archive, 1971 by its copyright notice. 'a good drummer; qualified to play anything': a military band, a society band, Dixieland. Knows five-four and seven, 'and I also know where to start'. 'I don't want my band to sound like his' (Basie). Rock: 'The good things are great; the other stuff is junk.' Max Roach and Art Blakey 'played with great intensity, feeling and command of the instrument.' Against taking 'the heads off the drums'.

title: Todd Bishop, 'Transcription: Buddy Rich - Big Mac' (Cruise Ship Drummer, 18 February 2023)
notes: Big Mac (Ernie Wilkins), from Ease On Down the Road; better known from The Roar of '74. 'Tempo is 93, the solo begins at 3:49.' 'I believe the stickings on the denser stuff are mostly singles'; 32nds and sextuplets in double-time passages. 'he's extremely aggressive with his accents'; 'It's Buddy, so lots of rim shots'; 'more unisons between the snare drum and bass drum than perhaps with other drummers'; 'Very little left foot activity that I can hear'; 'very thin little hihats' and a bright 20-inch A. Zildjian ride. 'It's a powerful sound but kind of crude'; 'His rock thing doesn't sound fully formed'. Only the prose was read, not the PDF.

title: Todd Bishop, 'Very occasional quote of the day: Buddy's time' (Cruise Ship Drummer, 3 March 2018), quoting bassist Chuck Bergeron
notes: Bergeron, bassist in the 1980s band, asked whether Rich wanted the time more 'on top'; Rich pointed to his heart: 'I want it RIGHT HERE, right down the middle'. Bergeron: 'the only definitive place to put the time is right down the middle and with conviction.'

title: Shelly Manne on Buddy Rich (Down Beat, March 1973), quoted in Cruise Ship Drummer, 28 January 2026
notes: 'I think Buddy Rich is a stupendous drummer, and I have the utmost respect for him.' 'But I don't really retain anything Buddy plays.' 'He only reaches my head. He doesn't reach my heart and soul.'

title: Greyson Nekrutman, '5 Impossible Buddy Rich Licks' (Drumeo Beat, 4 February 2022)
notes: Read through the WordPress API (post 33353). 1: 'Impossible Drum Solo' (1982): 'it's just a single stroke roll!' 2: Live in Tokyo (1964, Harry James): 'based on paradiddles, paradiddle-diddles, doubles and singles'. 3: Live in The Hague (1978): 'focuses heavily on the ride cymbal', singles, the bass drum landing with the cymbal at the end. 4: Live in The Hague (1978): 'This 'one-handed roll' is actually a group of three strokes on the left hand', then the bass drum or floor tom; both hands together on 1. 5: Live in Copenhagen (1968): 'the classic break in Buddy Rich's 'Love For Sale'', single strokes with accents. Singles go from wrist to fingers as the tempo rises. The note values of each lick were not given in the text.

title: Scott K. Fish, 'Ed Soph - Buddy Rich Was a Genius' (scottkfish.com, 11 July 2023)
notes: Soph's letter: Ray Brown named Rich the drummer he most enjoyed: 'We both felt the time in the same place, on-top-of-the beat.' At a Dorsey rehearsal a singer complained the drummer was not reading his charts; at the show Rich played figures the singer had not known could be played. Brown called him 'the only musical genius he had ever met.' Soph: people miss 'the vast scope of his genius'; the bassless trio records with Nat King Cole and Lester Young.

title: David Ingamells, '10 of The Best Buddy Rich Albums in Jazz History' (Jazzfuel, updated 26 January 2026)
notes: His style 'was characterised by playing along with a lot of the melodies, as opposed to playing around them', which 'forced the other musicians to play their parts like a drummer'. Joined Dorsey in 1939; Anatomy of a Jam Session (1945); The Engine Room (1946); Bird (1950); The Drum Battle (Krupa and Rich at JATP, 1952); Swingin' New Big Band (1966); Mercy, Mercy (1968); The Roar of '74: Nutville 'blurs the lines between Latin, funk and swing styles'.

title: Buddy Rich - Bernard Rich (jazz.com encyclopedia)
notes: 'dexterous use of difficult rhythmic devices with an ability to accompany any melody with great precision'; 'created a modern sound for the big band'; brushes behind Parker on Just Friends (Charlie Parker with Strings, 1949); 'incorporated influences from bebop and rock and roll'.

title: Jim Warchol, 'Buddy Rich' (Modern Drummer, January 1977)
notes: Only the opening was readable (paywall). 'Colossal technique combined with total control and dynamic propelling drive'; 'fiery fills and subtle nuances'; 'The left hand, always active, interacting with astonishing bass drum work.'

title: 'Slightly Offbeat: Buddy Rich, Meet Eric Fischer' (Modern Drummer, April 2010; posted 23 February 2010)
notes: Fischer transcribed Rich's solos with Tommy Dorsey on The Trombone Man Is the Best Man in the Band (1941, the film Las Vegas Nights) and Not So Quiet Please (dated 1948 there), checked against MIDI laid over the footage. The PDFs were not read.

title: Swingin' New Big Band - Wikipedia
notes: Pacific Jazz PJ 10113 / ST 20113, 1966. Gene Quill, Peter Yellin, Jay Corre, Martin Flax, Stephen Perlow (reeds); Bobby Shew, John Sottile, Yoshito Murakami, Walter Battegello (trumpets); Jim Trimble, John Boice, Dennis Good, Mike Waverley (trombones); John Bunch (piano), Barry Zweig (guitar), Carson Smith (bass), Buddy Rich (drums). Ready Mix, Basically Blues, Critic's Choice, My Man's Gone Now, Uptight, Sister Sadie, More Soul, and the West Side Story medley (10:48). Arrangers Bill Holman, Oliver Nelson, Don Piestrup, Don Rader, Bill Reddie and others. 1996 CD adds Apples (a.k.a. Gino) and eight more.

title: Big Swing Face (Buddy Rich album) - Wikipedia
notes: Pacific Jazz, June 1967; recorded live at the Chez, Hollywood, 22-25 February and 10 March 1967. Norwegian Wood, Big Swing Face, Monitor Theme, Wack Wack, Love for Sale, Mexicali Nose, Willowcrest, The Beat Goes On (Cathy Rich, vocals overdubbed), Bugle Call Rag.

title: Mercy, Mercy (Buddy Rich album) - Wikipedia
notes: Pacific Jazz ST 20133; recorded 7 July 1968 at Caesars Palace, Las Vegas. Mercy, Mercy, Mercy; Preach and Teach; Channel One Suite (Bill Reddie, 12:50); Big Mama Cass; Goodbye Yesterday; Acid Truth; Alfie; Ode to Billie Joe; 1997 CD adds Chavala, Mr. Lucky and Chelsea Bridge. Art Pepper, Charles Owens, Don Menza, Pat LaBarbera, John Laws; Al Porcino; Joe Azarello (piano), Walter Namuth (guitar), Gary Walters (bass).

title: Rich Versus Roach - Wikipedia
notes: Mercury MG-20448; recorded 7-8 April 1959; producer Jack Tracy. Rich's quintet (Phil Woods, Willie Dennis, John Bunch, Phil Leshin) on the left channel, Roach's (Tommy and Stanley Turrentine, Julian Priester, Bobby Boswell) on the right. Sing, Sing, Sing; The Casbah; Sleep; Figure Eights; Yesterdays; Big Foot; Limehouse Blues; Toot, Toot, Tootsie, Goodbye.

title: Krupa and Rich - Wikipedia
notes: Clef MGC 684, produced by Norman Granz; recorded 1 November 1955. Buddy's Blues, Bernie's Tune, Gene's Blues, Sweethearts on Parade, I Never Knew. Each drummer plays on two tracks alone; Bernie's Tune (13:54) is the one on which they play together. Oscar Peterson, Ray Brown, Herb Ellis, Roy Eldridge, Dizzy Gillespie, Illinois Jacquet, Flip Phillips.

title: The Roar of '74 - Wikipedia
notes: Groove Merchant 528; recorded 6 and 13 October 1973, Bell Sound, New York; producer Sonny Lester. Nutville, Kilimanjaro Cookout, Big Mac, Backwoods Sideman, Time Check, Prelude to a Kiss, Waltz of the Mushroom Hunters, Senator Sam. Tony Levin (electric bass), Joe Beck (guitar), Jimmy Maeulen (conga), Sam Woodyard (percussion). DownBeat (James Schaffer): Rich takes no solos; 'a total concept of no real 'stars,' just a very tight, hard-driving band.'

title: Rich a la Rakha - Wikipedia
notes: World Pacific WPS-21453; recorded 5 February 1968. Rich on drums, dholak and dholki; Alla Rakha, tabla; Ravi Shankar conducting; Paul Horn, flute. Khanda Kafi; Duet in Dadra (Rakha, Rich); Rangeela; Nagma E Raksh; Tal Sawari (Rakha, Rich, 14:30). The page says nothing of the meters or of how the two drummers interlock.

title: Burning for Buddy: A Tribute to the Music of Buddy Rich - Wikipedia
notes: Released 4 October 1994; recorded May 1994, Power Station, New York; produced by Neil Peart. The Buddy Rich Big Band with Simon Phillips, Dave Weckl, Steve Gadd, Matt Sorum, Steve Smith, Neil Peart, Manu Katche, Mino Cinelu, Billy Cobham, Max Roach, Rod Morgenstein, Kenny Aronoff, Omar Hakim, Ed Shaughnessy, Joe Morello, Bill Bruford, Marvin 'Smitty' Smith, Steve Ferrone. Volume 2 in 1997.

title: Buddy Rich Big Band, North Sea Jazz Festival, The Hague, 14 July 1978 (Dutch television, 'World of Jazz'; AVROTROS archive)
notes: Channel One Suite, 14 July 1978 (also https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iEt4XB-6dKY, the full concert). Watched in frames: the band in navy blazers on risers before the festival's logo; Rich at the front left on a low riser, in a navy V-neck pullover over a white shirt with long collar points spread over it, cream trousers, short dark hair; a white marine pearl kit with chrome hardware, a white front head on the bass drum with a 'BR' monogram, one tom on the bass drum, a floor tom with a tan towel on it, ride over the floor tom, crash at the left; an Ampeg bass amplifier behind him.

title: Buddy Rich Big Band, TV studio, Copenhagen, 1968 (black-and-white Danish television)
notes: Watched in frames (1:00-3:00): an interview close-up in a light jacket over a dark open shirt, then the band's title card and the band on a TV set. The source of Drumeo's Love for Sale lick (Live in Copenhagen, 1968).
